Algebraic fractions appear every year, between Q7 and Q12, and simplifying is a step inside a longer question rather than a question of its own: Summer 2023 Q9 (4 marks) was a subtraction then a division, Summer 2024 Q8(a) (4 marks) a division of two fractions, and Summer 2025 Q7 (7 marks) a subtraction then a division in one part. traps: Not factorising first, so cubic numerators and denominators appear and nothing can be cancelled (Summer 2018 Q8)
Cancelling a term of a sum rather than a factor, which changes the value of the expression (Summer 2018 Q8, Summer 2024 Q8)
Missing a difference of two squares, especially with a number in front such as 4x² − 1 (Summer 2022 Q9(b)); a plain one such as x² − 4 inside a longer question was missed too (Summer 2023 Q9)
Stopping before the numerical factor has been cancelled, so 2 over 4 is left on the answer line (Summer 2024 Q8(a), where a high number of candidates missed the factor of 2)
Leaving an x that is still a factor of both lines (Summer 2023 Q9)
Dividing the numerator by a constant before factorising, which loses a factor (Summer 2019 Q12)
Multiplying the brackets out instead of leaving the answer factorised, which hides whatever is left in common
Stopping one step short of a whole-number answer: Summer 2025 Q7 simplified to 2, and many left it in factorised form

noteBlocks.caption: A factor multiplies the whole line and can be struck; a term is only added, and striking it changes the value.

noteBlocks.md: Cancelling is division: it divides the top and the bottom by the same thing, which leaves the value alone. In the drawing, $\frac{6 \times 2}{6 \times 3}$ loses its 6s and becomes $\frac{2}{3}$, the same number. In $\frac{6+2}{6 \times 3}$ the 6 on top is only added: striking it would turn $\frac{8}{18}$ into $\frac{2}{3}$, a different number.
So only a **factor** can go: something the whole line is multiplied by. A **term** is added to the rest of its line, and dividing it alone does not divide the line.

noteBlocks.stem: Does the $x$ divide out of $\dfrac{x(x+8)}{5x}$, and out of $\dfrac{x+8}{5x}$?

steps.decision: Here the $x$ multiplies the whole top and the whole bottom: a factor of both lines, so it divides out.
Here the $x$ on top is added to the 8: a term. Test the fraction with a number first.
A cancel must leave the value alone. This one changes it, so the $x$ stays where it is.

noteBlocks.explain: Cancelling divides a whole line, so only a factor can go. In $\frac{x+4}{x}$ the $x$ on top is added to the 4, a term, as in step 2 of the See it, and no 4 sits underneath. Test it as step 3 did: at $x=1$ the fraction is 5, not 4 or 1. So nothing cancels.

optionNotes.why: It looks like an $x$ over an $x$, but the $x$ on top is only added to the 4, so striking it changes the value: at $x=1$ the fraction is 5, not 4.
Striking both treats each term as a factor, but neither multiplies the whole top and no 4 sits underneath: at $x=1$ the value would drop from 5 to 1.

twin.explain: The 2 multiplies the whole top and 6 is $2 \times 3$, so the 2 divides out of both lines. Inside the bracket, $x$ and 9 are terms added together, as in step 2 of the See it, so neither the $x$ nor a 3 from the 9 can go.

optionNotes.why: The $x$ underneath seems to match the one in the bracket, but that $x$ is added to 9, a term, so striking it changes the value.
9 and 3 do share a 3, but the 9 is only added to $x$, so a 3 cannot come out of the whole top.

noteBlocks.caption: Factorise the top, factorise the bottom, strike what both share: 7x + 35 over x² + 5x is 7 over x.

noteBlocks.md: The paper never hands you brackets. In the drawing, $7x+35$ and $x^{2}+5x$ show nothing in common until each is factorised; then $(x+5)$ appears on both lines and cancels, leaving $\frac{7}{x}$.

So every simplification is the same three moves. Factorise the top fully, common factor first. Factorise the bottom the same way. Then strike every factor both lines share, numbers included, and check that nothing else divides both.

On the scheme each factorised line earns an MW1, a mark for method and accurate working, and the last mark, a W1, is for the finished answer. So write each factorised line on its own, even when you can see the answer.

steps.decision: Take out what both terms of the top share: 5.
Both terms of the bottom carry an $x$, so it comes out.
$(x+3)$ multiplies the whole top and the whole bottom, so it divides out. 5 and $x$ share nothing, so this is fully simplified.
Check with a number: the question and the answer give the same value.

noteBlocks.title: Simplifying Algebraic Fractions
noteBlocks.why: The same three moves at writing speed, on several shapes that the sections below take one at a time. Watch it once, then try the Your turn without going back.

noteBlocks.explain: Factorise both lines first, as steps 1 and 2 of the See it did: $4x+24=4(x+6)$ and $x^{2}+6x=x(x+6)$. Then $(x+6)$ divides out of both, leaving $\frac{4}{x}$. Stopping at the factorised line leaves $(x+6)$ on both lines, and striking $x$ from single terms changes the value.

optionNotes.why: Both lines are factorised, which earns the method marks, but $(x+6)$ is still on the top and the bottom, so the last move is not done.
Dividing only some terms by $x$ changes the fraction: $4x$ lost its $x$ but 24 did not, and only a factor of a whole line can go.

twin.explain: Factorised, the top is $3(x+10)$ and the bottom $x(x+10)$, as in steps 1 and 2 of the See it. The bracket is a factor of both lines and divides out, leaving $\frac{3}{x}$.

optionNotes.why: The factorising is done, but $(x+10)$ is still on both lines, so one more cancel is due.
Taking an $x$ out of $3x$ but not out of 30 changes the fraction; only a factor of the whole line can go.

noteBlocks.caption: The L-shape has area x² − a². Move its shaded strip and it becomes a rectangle x + a long, x − a wide.

noteBlocks.md: In the drawing, the square $x^{2}$ loses the corner $a^{2}$, and the strip that moves round turns what is left into a rectangle $x+a$ long and $x-a$ wide. So a square minus a square always splits into two brackets, one plus and one minus: $x^{2}-a^{2}=(x+a)(x-a)$.

Multiply back to check: $(x+a)(x-a)=x^{2}-ax+ax-a^{2}$, and the two middle terms cancel. That is why this shape never has an $x$ term. Look for it whenever a line has two terms, a minus between them, and a square on each side of the minus.

steps.decision: Two terms, a minus, and $64=8^{2}$: a square minus a square.
The top has a common factor of 3.
$(x+8)$ is a factor of both lines, so it divides out; $(x-8)$ stays underneath.
The check agrees.

noteBlocks.prompt: What is $x^{2}-81$ as a product of two brackets?
noteBlocks.explain: Eighty-one is $9^{2}$, so $x^{2}-81$ is a square minus a square, as in step 1 of the See it: one bracket takes $+9$, the other $-9$, and the middle terms cancel. $(x+9)^{2}$ gives $x^{2}+18x+81$, and $(x+81)(x-1)$ gives $x^{2}+80x-81$. So it is $(x+9)(x-9)$.

optionNotes.why: 81 is a square, so a squared bracket feels right, but $(x+9)^{2}$ multiplies out to $x^{2}+18x+81$: a plus and an $x$ term the line does not have.
81 and $-1$ do multiply to $-81$, but they add to 80, which gives an $80x$ term; a square minus a square needs $+9$ and $-9$.

twin.prompt: What is $x^{2}-400$ as a product of two brackets?
twin.explain: 400 is $20^{2}$, so $x^{2}-400$ is a square minus a square, as in step 1 of the See it: $(x+20)(x-20)$, whose middle terms cancel. $(x-20)^{2}$ has a $-40x$ term, and $(x+400)(x-1)$ a $399x$ term.

optionNotes.why: A squared bracket multiplies out to $x^{2}-40x+400$, with an $x$ term and $+400$ where the line has $-400$.
400 and $-1$ multiply to $-400$ but add to 399, so an $x$ term appears; the pair must be $+20$ and $-20$.

noteBlocks.md: When the $x^{2}$ carries a square number, split it the same way, taking the square root of each part. The root of $25x^{2}$ is $5x$, not $25x$, because $5x$ times $5x$ is $25x^{2}$. In the drawing the big square has side $5x$ and the corner side 2, so the rectangle is $5x+2$ by $5x-2$.
Summer 2022 examiners often saw $4x^{2}-1$ left unfactorised inside a longer question, so look for this shape whenever both terms are squares.

steps.decision: $25x^{2}=(5x)^{2}$ and $4=2^{2}$: a square minus a square, as in the drawing.
Both terms of the bottom carry an $x$.
$(5x-2)$ divides out of both lines. The 5 in $5x$ multiplies only the $x$, and the 2 is added, so nothing else cancels.
The check agrees.

noteBlocks.explain: Take the square root of each part, as step 1 of the See it did: $36x^{2}=(6x)^{2}$ and $25=5^{2}$, so the brackets hold $6x$ and 5, one plus and one minus. $(36x+5)(36x-5)$ would start $1296x^{2}$, and $(6x+5)^{2}$ has a middle term, $60x$. So it is $(6x+5)(6x-5)$.

optionNotes.why: Putting $36x$ in the bracket forgets the square root: $36x$ times $36x$ is $1296x^{2}$, not $36x^{2}$.
A squared bracket gives $36x^{2}+60x+25$, with a middle term and a plus, so it is not a square minus a square.

twin.explain: $49x^{2}=(7x)^{2}$ and $9=3^{2}$, so the brackets hold $7x$ and 3, one plus and one minus, as in step 1 of the See it. $(49x+3)(49x-3)$ starts $2401x^{2}$, and $(7x-3)^{2}$ has a $-42x$ term.

optionNotes.why: $49x$ in the bracket forgets the square root: $49x$ times $49x$ is $2401x^{2}$.
A squared bracket gives $49x^{2}-42x+9$, with a middle term and $+9$ where the line has $-9$.

noteBlocks.caption: Both pieces are 3x tall, so 3x² + 30x is 3x lots of (x + 10): the shared side is the common factor.

noteBlocks.md: Before any brackets, look for what every term shares: a number, an $x$, or both. In the drawing both pieces are $3x$ tall, so $3x^{2}+30x=3x(x+10)$. Taking the common factor out first often uncovers two squares.
Keep the number you take out: it is a factor of the whole line, not something to divide away. Summer 2019 candidates who divided by 3 before factorising lost that 3 from their answer.

noteBlocks.title: Beyond this specification
noteBlocks.md: The statement names linear and quadratic numerators and denominators, and no FM1 paper from 2018 to 2026 sets a cubic to factorise; the cubic terms in 2019 Q12(ii) cancel once the top is collected. If one ever appears, the first move is the same: take out the common factor.

steps.decision: Both terms share 2, so it comes out first. What is left inside is two squares.
$196=14^{2}$: a square minus a square. The 2 stays in front.
The bottom's common factor is $x$.
Strike $(x+14)$ from both lines and keep the 2: it multiplies the whole top.
The check agrees, minus signs and all.

noteBlocks.explain: Take the 2 out first, as steps 1 and 2 of the See it did: $2x^{2}-512=2(x+16)(x-16)$, and the bottom is $x(x+16)$. Strike $(x+16)$ and keep the 2, which multiplies the whole top. Stopping at $2(x^{2}-256)$ hides the bracket that cancels.

optionNotes.why: Dropping the 2 feels like simplifying, but it multiplies the whole top, so dividing it away halves the value.
$x^{2}-256$ looks finished, but it is still a square minus a square; until it splits, the $(x+16)$ that cancels stays hidden.

twin.explain: Take the 3 out: $3x^{2}-192=3(x^{2}-64)=3(x+8)(x-8)$, as steps 1 and 2 of the See it did, and the bottom is $x(x+8)$. Strike $(x+8)$ and keep the 3.

optionNotes.why: The 3 multiplies the whole top, so dropping it divides the value by 3.
$x^{2}-64$ still splits into $(x+8)(x-8)$, and only then can $(x+8)$ cancel.

noteBlocks.caption: x² + 9x + 20 laid out as a rectangle: the strips 5x and 4x make 9x, and 4 × 5 = 20.

noteBlocks.md: In the drawing, $x^{2}+9x+20$ laid out as a rectangle is $x+5$ long and $x+4$ wide. The two strips, $4x$ and $5x$, make the $9x$, and the corner is $4 \times 5=20$. So look for two numbers that multiply to the constant and add to the $x$ coefficient.
Multiply back to check the signs. When the two numbers are the same, the line is a perfect square, one bracket squared: over a fraction line one of its brackets can cancel, and the other stays.

steps.decision: $4 \times 5=20$ and $4+5=9$, as in the drawing.
$4 \times 4=16$ and $4+4=8$: the same number twice, so a perfect square.
One $(x+4)$ divides out of each line; the other $(x+4)$ stays underneath.
The check agrees.

noteBlocks.explain: Factorise first, as steps 1 and 2 of the See it did: the top is $(x+8)(x+3)$ and the bottom $(x+8)(x-3)$, so $(x+8)$ divides out. Striking the two $x^{2}$ terms cancels terms of a sum, and stopping at the factorised line leaves $(x+8)$ on both lines.

optionNotes.why: Everything is factorised, but $(x+8)$ sits on both lines, so the cancel that earns the last mark is still to do.
The $x^{2}$ on each line looks like a match, but each is only one term of a sum, so striking them changes the value.

twin.explain: The top is $(x+9)(x+4)$ and the bottom $(x+9)(x-4)$, as steps 1 and 2 of the See it would find. Strike $(x+9)$ from both lines to leave $\frac{x+4}{x-4}$.

optionNotes.why: The factorising is right, but $(x+9)$ is still on both lines, so it is not finished.
Striking the $x^{2}$ terms cancels parts of two sums, which changes the value; only whole factors cancel.

noteBlocks.caption: 2x² + 9x + 10 as a rectangle: the strips 4x and 5x make 9x, and 4 × 5 = 2 × 10.

noteBlocks.md: With a number in front of $x^{2}$ the brackets start differently. In the drawing, $2x^{2}+9x+10$ is a rectangle $2x+5$ long and $x+2$ wide. Its strips, $4x$ and $5x$, make the $9x$, and $4 \times 5=20$, which is $2 \times 10$: the number in front times the constant.

So multiply the number in front by the constant, find two numbers with that product and the $x$ coefficient as their sum, and split the middle term with them. Then factorise in pairs, and expand to check.
This shape is no rarity on FM1: Summer 2021 ($2x^{2}-x-1$), 2022 ($2x^{2}+x-1$), 2024 ($2x^{2}+3x-5$) and 2026 ($2x^{2}+5x+3$) each set one inside a longer question.

steps.decision: $2 \times 10=20$, and 4 and 5 multiply to 20 and add to 9, so split $9x$ into $4x+5x$.
Factorise each pair; the shared $(x+2)$ comes out. Expand to check: $2x^{2}+4x+5x+10$.
The bottom's common factor is $x$.
Strike $(x+2)$. The 2 in $2x$ multiplies only the $x$, not the whole top, so it stays.
The check agrees.

noteBlocks.explain: Split the middle term as step 1 of the See it did: $2 \times (-3)=-6$, and 6 and $-1$ multiply to $-6$ and add to 5. So $2x^{2}+6x-x-3=2x(x+3)-(x+3)=(2x-1)(x+3)$. $(2x+3)(x-1)$ expands to $2x^{2}+x-3$, and $(2x+1)(x-3)$ to $2x^{2}-5x-3$.

optionNotes.why: 3 and $-1$ multiply to $-3$, but with $2x$ in front the middle term comes out as $x$, not $5x$: the pair must multiply to $2 \times (-3)=-6$.
The numbers are right but the signs are swapped, so the middle term comes out as $-5x$; expand to check the sign.

twin.explain: $3 \times 2=6$, and 6 and 1 multiply to 6 and add to 7, as step 1 of the See it found its pair. So $3x^{2}+6x+x+2=3x(x+2)+(x+2)=(3x+1)(x+2)$. $(3x+2)(x+1)$ gives $5x$ in the middle, and $(3x-1)(x-2)$ gives $-7x$.

optionNotes.why: 2 and 1 multiply to 2, but with $3x$ in front the middle term is $5x$, not $7x$: the pair must multiply to $3 \times 2=6$.
Both signs are minus, so the middle term comes out as $-7x$ where the line has $+7x$.

noteBlocks.md: The instruction is **simplify fully**, and the last mark goes on that word. Fully means nothing at all still divides both lines: no bracket, no number and no lone $x$. In the drawing all three kinds are struck, and what is left is 3.

noteBlocks.title: Why a lone number or x still counts
noteBlocks.md: A 2 over a 4, or an $x$ over an $x$, divides the whole top and the whole bottom just as a bracket does, so it is a common factor too. When every factor of the bottom divides away, no fraction line is left: FM1's answers were $2x$ in 2021, $3(x-2)$ in 2023 and 2 in 2025.

noteBlocks.title: Summer 2024, FM1 Q8(a)
noteBlocks.md: Most candidates factorised every expression and cancelled correctly, and then a high number stopped one step early, leaving a factor of 2 in the answer. The algebra was right, and the final mark was lost.

steps.decision: Everything the two terms share comes out: 9 and $x$.
The same for the bottom: 3 and $x$.
Strike the bracket $(x-5)$ from both lines. Not finished: two more factors are shared.
The numbers: 9 and 3 share a 3.
The lone $x$ divides both lines too. Nothing is left underneath, so the answer has no fraction line.
The check agrees; the fraction is 3 for every $x$ it allows.

noteBlocks.explain: Look at the numbers, as step 4 of the See it did: 14 and 7 share a factor of 7, so dividing both by 7 gives $\frac{2}{x-9}$. Multiplying the bracket out to $\frac{14}{7x-63}$ only hides that factor. So no: it becomes $\frac{2}{x-9}$.

optionNotes.why: With the bracket already on its own it looks finished, but 14 and 7 still share a factor of 7.
Multiplying out looks like progress, but it only hides the shared 7: $7x-63$ is still $7(x-9)$.

twin.explain: 18 and 6 share a factor of 6, as the numbers did in step 4 of the See it, so dividing both by 6 gives $\frac{3}{x-4}$. Multiplying the bracket out to $\frac{18}{6x-24}$ only hides that factor.

optionNotes.why: The bracket is simplified, but 18 and 6 still share a factor of 6.
Multiplying out hides the shared 6 rather than removing it: $6x-24$ is still $6(x-4)$.

Removing the $x$ underneath without dividing the top by $x$ as well changes the value: at $x=2$, 12 becomes 24.

**'Simplest form' means fully.** A question asking for one fraction in its simplest form (2018, 2022) wants what **simplify fully** wants. Fully never means multiplying out: 2022's answer was $\frac{5(2x+1)}{x+1}$, brackets and all.

items.stem: What is the first move when you simplify $\frac{x^{2}+11x+30}{x^{2}+x-30}$?

options.text: Factorise the top and the bottom
options.feedback: Always. Until both lines are products, there is nothing that can legitimately be cancelled.

options.text: Cancel the $x^{2}$ on the top with the $x^{2}$ on the bottom
options.feedback: Those are terms of a sum, so they cannot be cancelled. Factorise first: the top is $(x+5)(x+6)$ and the bottom $(x+6)(x-5)$, and then $(x+6)$ may go.

options.text: Divide every term on both lines by $x$
options.feedback: Dividing through by $x$ leaves fractions inside the expression and hides the factors. Factorise first and the common bracket appears on its own.

items.skill: Recognise a difference of two squares with a coefficient

options.feedback: $9x^{2}-25$ is $9x^{2}$ minus $25$, so it is $(3x)^{2}-5^{2}$ and the two brackets are $(3x-5)$ and $(3x+5)$.
Multiply that out and the $x^{2}$ term is $81x^{2}$. The square root of $9x^{2}$ is $3x$, not $9x$.
That is $9x^{2}-30x+25$, which has a middle term. A difference of two squares has no middle term because the two cross terms cancel.

items.stem: Kara has reached $\frac{6}{3(x-3)}$ when simplifying $\frac{6x+18}{3x^{2}-27}$. What still has to happen?

options.feedback: The brackets are done and the numbers are not: the 6 and the 3 still share a 3. The last mark goes to the fully simplified answer, so the numbers have to be finished too.

options.text: Nothing more — it is already fully simplified
options.feedback: The 6 and the 3 share a factor of 3, so this is not fully simplified yet. Summer 2024 examiners reported a high number of candidates losing the last mark by leaving a factor of 2 in an answer.
Multiplying out hides the factors and does not simplify anything. The bracket form is what lets you see the last common factor.

items.skill: Tell a perfect square from a difference of two squares

options.feedback: The two numbers multiply to $49$ and add to $14$, so both are $7$ and the quadratic is a perfect square.
That is $x^{2}-49$, which has no $x$ term. A plus sign in front of the $14x$ means both brackets carry $+7$.
It does. Look for two numbers with product $49$ and sum $14$; $7$ and $7$ work, and they always will when the quadratic is a perfect square.

items.skill: Factorise both lines, then cancel one bracket

options.feedback: The top is $(x+10)(x-10)$ and the bottom is $(x+10)^{2}$, so one $(x+10)$ divides out of each line.
The two $x^{2}$ terms have been struck out, and they are terms of a sum, not factors. Factorise first: the top is $(x+10)(x-10)$ and the bottom is $(x+10)^{2}$.
The bottom is factorised and the top is not, so no common bracket can be seen. Factorise both lines before you look for anything to cancel.

items.skill: Simplify all the way, to a whole number if that is what is left

options.feedback: The bracket $(x+9)$ has gone, but an $x$ still divides both lines. Strike it too and $4$ is left.
Dividing only the top by $4$ changes the fraction's value. Factorise instead: the top is $4x(x+9)$ and the bottom $x(x+9)$, so $4$ is left.
The top is $4x(x+9)$ and the bottom is $x(x+9)$. Both $x$ and $(x+9)$ divide out, and a whole number is left.
